content.title: Understanding the Pavement Program
content.summary: Arvada's Pavement Management Program is crucial for maintaining the city's extensive street network, which spans over 1,500 lane miles and is valued at over $1 billion. With an annual budget of approximately $15 million, the program focuses on preventative maintenance to extend road life and reduce future repair costs, although it faces challenges due to limited funding against the backdrop of an aging infrastructure. The city assesses road quality every three years to prioritize maintenance efforts and ensure effective use of public funds.
content.body:
![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=5927)

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=5924)

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=5930)

Arvada **community members continue to rank street maintenance as one of the most important services that the City provides**in the [annual Community Survey](/238). The City owns a street network of over 1,500 lane miles, valued at over $1 billion, making it one of the largest and most high-value assets within the city.

The Pavement Management Program (Program) plays a vital role in the maintenance and rehabilitation of our streets. **The City team is committed to stretching every dollar as much as possible to effectively maintain and improve roads.**With a limited budget of about $15 million annually to maintain a network valued at over 70 times that, the Program can face challenges to address all of the streets that are aging or in poor condition.

This page shares information about the Program to help increase understanding and transparency around how the street network is managed and how work is funded. **For information about work taking place this year,** please [visit the main Pavement Program webpage](/629).

## Life cycle of a road

The most cost effective way to extend the life of a road is through routine maintenance on roads in good conditions. As roads fall into disrepair, they deteriorate faster and become much more expensive to rehabilitate or reconstruct.

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=5856)**On average, every $1 spent on preventative maintenance can save $4 to $5 in future repair costs.**

Today, the Pavement Program spends a budget of approximately $15 million annually on preventative maintenance, rehabilitation, and adjacent concrete repairs.

### Life cycle phases

- New construction or reconstructed road (years 1-5)
- Preventative maintenance work (years 3-15): $6,000 to $90,000 per lane mile
- Major rehabilitation work (years 15-25): $134,000 to $198,000 per lane mile
- Reconstruction (years 25+): $370,000 to $550,000 per lane mile

## Road quality in Arvada

Each City-owned street is assessed every three years to maintain accurate information about the quality of the road network, this is called the Pavement Quality Index (PQI). PQI helps the Pavement Management team decide which streets to work on each year and what type of work is needed.

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=5858)This bell curve shows the distribution of our road network quality from 0 to 100 PQI with the current network average, the peak of the curve, near 40 PQI. The City's goal is to have a network average of 70 PQI represented with the green line.

While this status is lower than desired, this information helps the team prioritize how to spend a limited budget. Generally, streets with high speed limits and more traffic rise to a higher priority level but the team also balances those needs with work on local, neighborhood roads.

- **Curious how Arvada roads compare to neighboring cities?**
- **Wondering why some roads are prioritized higher?**
- **Interested in how road quality may affect you?**

[Learn more in the FAQs below!](#FAQs)

## Funding the program

Much like regular car maintenance is a cost effective way to extend the life of your car, regular road maintenance and rehabilitation helps extend the life of a road. Once a road falls into disrepair, more cost intensive reconstruction work is needed, similar to needing to buy a new car!

**The City is committed to maintaining and improving streets through transparent and responsible spending of public funds.**As program costs continue to increase, the Program funding is challenged to keep up with and effectively address the needs of an aging street network.

### Funding sources

The Program receives funding from the City’s general fund, made up largely of tax revenues that are distributed to the City. The City collects:

- 3.46% sales and use taxes ($0.0346 of every $1)
- 4.31 mills in property tax ($4.31 for every $1000)
- Highway User Tax Fund (HUTF) distributed through the state based on population size (approximately $4 million annually)

All tax revenues brought into the City are managed through a 10-year budget plan with a 2-year budget cycle and annual adjustments. A portion of what is collected is distributed to the Pavement Program to make up their $15 Million annual budget.

### Funding history

When available, the City distributes a portion of additional revenue over the budgeted amount to the Pavement Program. These one-time funds are contingent on the City bringing in more revenue than projected. While the City makes conservative projections, this is not a guaranteed source of additional funds and has not been sufficient to sustainably supplement the Program budget.

This graph shows the change in program funding from 2010 to 2025 from less than $5 million to just over $15 million. The bars combine increases to the on-going maintenance budget over time and the additional one-time funds in some years to create the total budget for each year.

- **Could more funding be redistributed to the program?**[See the FAQs!](#FAQs)

### Current and ideal funding

**Today, the Program continues to balance spending needs as much as possible to apply cost effective treatments to maintain roads in good condition while also addressing roads that are falling into poor condition.**These roads require more cost intensive rehabilitation and reconstruction work. The current budget is not keeping pace with these needs as more roads age and fall into poor conditions.

This chart breaks down annual work completed using 2024 numbers compared to the ideal status of the program to sustain needed maintenance practices and make substantial progress on streets that have fallen into disrepair.

| Type of Work | **Current (2024) funding** | **Ideal funding (to achieve 70 PQI)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
Current funding compared to the ideal funding amounts for certain types of work

| Maintenance | - 9% of the street network - 135 lane miles - $2 million | - 10-20% of the street network - 150-300 lane miles - $2.2 - $4.4 million |
| Rehabilitation | - 2.7% of the street network - 41 lane miles - $7.3 million | - 5% of the street network - 75 lane miles - $20 million |
| Concrete\* | - 3% of concrete adjacent to pavement work - $3.5 million | - 5% of concrete adjacent to pavement work - $8.8 million |
| Total cost | $13.5 million | $31-33 million |

\*Concrete work is funded through the Program when sidewalk, curb and gutter damage may affect the integrity of the future paving work or to replace curb ramps for compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

## Future planning

Improving the status of Arvada's road quality will take time. Sustained, increased funding can lead to steady progress over time. This would allow for a more robust mix of maintenance and rehabilitation strategies, extending pavement life and reducing costly reconstruction.

**Road quality, wherever it is, can affect your quality of life and as a City, we remain committed to this work.**

## Learn more

Listen to the Inside Arvada podcast episode about the Pavement Program using the player below or wherever you listen to podcasts, including [Apple](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/inside-arvada/id1736238466), [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/0NFHlh79S2aCYDX4zj8Crj), [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLJq_TITOXij3yXWNVlTKJBIQ-F8b3NeN2), and [Buzzsprout](https://www.buzzsprout.com/2320363/episodes/16782583-inside-arvada-s-pavement-program-with-ben-sawaya)(with transcript).

### [FAQs](/Faq.aspx?TID=97)

[How do Arvada's roads compare to other cities?](#)
:   Arvada’s Pavement Condition Index (PCI)\*, which measures road quality, is among the lowest in the Denver metro area and across Colorado. This map shows our road network average PCI in red compared with many of our neighboring cities in orange and green.

    ![map of metro Denver based on road quality averages showing Arvada in red](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=5857)

    \*Most cities report PCI as you see listed in this chart. This is one of several criteria measured to determine Pavement Quality Index (PQI). Arvada uses PQI which provides a more robust understanding of road quality.

    Text version of the chart information:

    - Golden: 84 PCI
    - Lakewood: 83 PCI
    - Denver: 80 PCI
    - Wheat Ridge: 78 PCI
    - Commerce City: 77 PCI
    - Broomfield: 75 PCI
    - Thornton: 73 PCI
    - Northglenn: 65 PCI
    - Westminster: 57 PCI
    - Arvada: 44 PCI

[Why are roads with more traffic and higher speed prioritized for work?](#)
:   Overall, the consequences of failure on these roads are higher. Roads with more traffic can deteriorate more quickly. The side-effects of poor road quality to vehicles and motorists when traveling at higher speeds are more severe.

[How does road quality affect me?](#)
:   Deficient road conditions in metro Denver can cost motorists over $3,000 annually, according to the [2025 Keeping Colorado Mobile](https://tripnet.org/reports/keeping-colorado-mobile-january-2025/) report from [TRIP](https://tripnet.org/). Beyond the comfort of your ride, poor road conditions can also affect factors like vehicle operating costs, congestion, and other safety issues that translate to costs to motorists.

[Can the City redistribute funding from other services?](#)
:   With the competing needs of other services, and rising costs today, an additional redistribution of funds would come with tradeoffs to other City services. This is not feasible to cover the program needs to make sufficient progress on improving the quality of Arvada’s roads. The City continues to prioritize distributing additional funding to the Program in two ways:

    - One-time fund requests if there are leftover funds in the annual budget at the end of a budget year.
    - A portion of additional revenues brought in over what the City budgeted for in a year.

    These funds are able to be spent in the following year to provide a small boost to the Program. However, these are not guaranteed, nor are they a sufficient or sustainable increase in funding to make consistent progress on improving the quality of the road network.
